title: Sanders and Casar introduce Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act with cabinet-level Department of AI
subtitle: The Senate–House bill would freeze advanced AI development until a new federal agency is up and running, and criminalize superintelligence work with penalties comparable to unlawful nuclear weapons.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and Representative Greg Casar (D-TX) introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act on September 23. The bill would stand up a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence led by a Secretary of AI, pause advanced-model development until that agency is operating and has issued binding safety rules, and permanently prohibit systems that surpass human cognitive performance across most domains. It also directs the executive branch to pursue international agreements aimed at preventing superintelligence from being built anywhere in the world. Violators face what the sponsors call a 'corporate death penalty' plus prison terms of up to 20 years, which Sanders explicitly compared to penalties for unlawfully building nuclear weapons.

The bill's mechanism matters more than its headline. Rather than layering rules onto existing agencies (FTC, NIST, Commerce), it creates a single vertically-integrated regulator with pre-deployment authority. That mirrors how the FDA regulates drugs and how the Nuclear Regulatory Commission regulates fissile material — categories where the sponsors argue frontier AI now belongs. The definition of 'superintelligence' the bill would ban is any system that exceeds human capability across a broad range of cognitive tasks; the definition of 'advanced AI' subject to the pause is broader and captures most frontier training runs currently in progress.

This is the second major legislative signal in a week. Days earlier, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic disclosed talks to stand up a voluntary Frontier AI Standards Agency with Sriram Krishnan as CEO — an industry-led attempt to preempt exactly this kind of statutory framework. The Sanders–Casar bill is unlikely to become law in the current Congress, but it establishes the maximalist policy pole: pause, criminalize, cabinet-level oversight. Every subsequent negotiation — including the industry standards body's charter and any future EU-US alignment — now has to price that position in.

Takeaway for learners: policy questions in AI are not going to be won by whoever has the best benchmark. If you plan to build or deploy frontier systems in the next five years, the regulatory scaffolding around your work will move faster than the models will. Read at least one live legislative proposal — this one, California's SB-53, the EU AI Act's GPAI thresholds — end to end. Knowing what a bill actually says, not what a headline claims it says, is a rarer skill than it should be.
